text:
anya: Heads up — prod-cluster-3 had a 3x OOM spike during a high-concurrency tail window last night. I sampled a few failures and the allocator traces show FlashAttention selecting a larger workspace because KV cache size jumped for some requests. Logs pasted below.

infra-bot: [ALERT] OOM on node g3-12x-07 at 2005549900. pid=1422, failed_alloc=1, free_mem=232MiB, requested=1.2GiB

ryan: link to the profile? can you drop the pprof or the allocator trace?

anya: gist: https://redwood/g/abc123 (profiling tarball). key snippet: 
```
alloc_trace: allocate(1_294_000_000) -> try_slab_alloc -> fragmentation=0.68 -> try_coalesce=false -> OOM
kernel_choice: flashattention_v2 workspace=1_200_000_000 (chosen because seq_len=2048 and batch=8)
kv_cache: per-request=810_000_000 total_kv_cached=3.2G
```

kevin: hmm ok. two orthogonal wins: (1) make allocator more willing to coalesce adjacent free slabs when a large workspace is needed, (2) enforce a soft per-request cap on KV cache growth during kernel selection so we don't let kernel chooser escalate workspace to an impossible size.

esther: soft cap risks correctness for long-context LLMs though. if we evict/limit KV aggressively we might truncate history and get hallucinations. any cap should be request-aware and be a soft preference, not a hard eviction.

zach: +1 on coalescer. fragmentation is the root cause here — we have a lot of mid-sized free blocks but nothing contiguous enough. a coalescing pass on allocation (or periodic defragmenter) could satisfy the big workspace without growing total memory. tradeoff is CPU and potential pause.

ryan: propose we add metrics: allocator.free_runs, allocator.coalesce_ops, allocator.coalesce_success_rate, failed_alloc_count, avg_fragmentation_ratio. use those to gate kernelchooser behavior.

anya: quick prototype idea for kernelchooser heuristic: if fragmentation_ratio > 0.6 and requested_workspace > free_contiguous * 1.1 then prefer memory-sparse kernel or reduce workspace target by kv_soft_cap factor. Pseudocode: 
```
if (frag_ratio > FRAG_THRESH) {
  workspace_target *= kv_soft_cap; // 0.8 default
  prefer_kernel(memory_sparse_kernel)
}
```

kevin: ran a local mini-bench with slab.coalesce enabled + kv_soft_cap=0.8: OOMs down ~18% across mixed shapes, tail p99 latency +2.3% avg. I'll drop raw numbers to the gist. Seems promising as config flags.

esther: also think about kernel-family fallback. Triton/cublaslt/cublas algorithms have different memory profiles; chooser should prefer the smaller-footprint kernel when fragmentation high even if nominal latency is slightly worse. evaluate with our standard prompt set.

zach: for allocator changes: implement immediate coalesce-on-alloc (coalesce adjacent free slabs until contiguous region >= needed) and an async background defrag pass that runs during low-util windows. also add metrics for coalesce attempts and time spent.

ryan: I'll prototype reclaim-on-alloc as well: if allocation fails, run a bounded async sweep to release reclaimable caches (prefix caches marked purgeable), then retry. we need safety throttles to avoid flapping.

anya: proposed rollout flags for initial canary: `slab.coalesce=true`, `allocator.coalesce_max_ms=4`, `kv.soft_cap=0.8`, `kernelchooser.fragmentation_threshold=0.6`, `kernelchooser.prefer_memory_sparse=true`. canary in us-east-1 Dedicated.

esther: :thumbsup: I can own canary evaluation and the quality regression suite. will run evals on the 10 canonical prompts (long-context + chat) and check for any perplexity/regression.

kevin: I'll open PR with allocator coalescer + unit tests. will include toggles and basic perf harness.

zach: let's ensure deferred coalesce doesn't create long-term fragmentation churn. add a max_coalesce_ops_per_second and a backoff.

deploy-bot: Canary scheduled: slab-coalesce-kvcap A/B in us-east-1 on Dedicated pool at 2005551800, canary window 1h.

anya: thanks all. next steps: kevin PR + benchmark numbers, ryan prototype reclaim-on-alloc, esther runs evals during canary, zach monitors fragmentation metrics. we'll reconvene after canary window. :eyes:
